newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain succumbs to Euro fever as budget impresses.
newsitem.headline: Spain succumbs to Euro fever as budget impresses.

text.p: Spain, once considered a long shot, is brimming with confidence that it will muscle into the elite group of nations founding the continent's common currency.

Brash and eager, the five-month-old minority government boasts it has drafted for 1997 one of the toughest budgets ever and brushes aside the dour warnings of the German Bundesbank on the hurdles to lasting stability.
"There is no one now who doubts that we will be in," Spanish prime minister Jose Maria Aznar told Congress on Wednesday.

Though typically skeptical, financial markets and economists have bought into the buoyant new attitude, overpowering domestic critics who worry the budget is lax in tackling the structural drains that will thwart fiscal discipline in years ahead.

"Confidence in the Spanish economy's convergence ability has risen considerably in recent months," Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said, mustering the government's most significant evidence of its success - soaring financial markets.

"Undoubtedly the government's liberalisation measures -- such as checks on public spending and guaranties on the fulfillment of the public deficit in 1996, and above all -- the presentation of an austere deficit are helping us from the market's point of view," he added.
The spread of Spanish bonds to German Bunds -- a measure of the added cost of holding riskier domestic issues -- has compressed dramatically in recent weeks.
The spread had more than halved to 156 basis points by Thursday from 330 on March 1. In the summer of 1995, the spread had gaped at 500.
The peseta continued its fight to break through 84.00 per mark -- with the market suspicion that only the Bank of Spain was holding it back -- despite last week's interest rate cut.
In a Reuter survey of 16 Spain-based analysts conducted earlier this week, nine forecast Spain would be in the Euro's launch, while two said it had a 50-50 chance.
Among the less optimistic, five predicted Spain would not make the first cut but three of those said it would manage to join a second round.
The crux of the latest rash of enthusiasm is the 1997 budget, which the government presented to Congress last week.
The draft has been viewed as a solid attempt to narrow the nation's deficit and installing fiscal discipline in the year that will serve as the litmus tests for the 1999 Euro launch.
The Bank of Spain gave its vote of confidence three days after the government presented the budget to parliament, cutting the official rate of money by 50 basis points to 6.75 percent.

In the Reuters poll, 12 said the budget was credible, but it appeared not to have escaped the wrath of the Bundesbank which is demanding ever more stridently that 1997 budgets set the base for durable fiscal discipline.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday in Bonn that, "The European Monetary Institute should not and will not let itself be blinded by one year's results. This is not a question of window-dressing, but rather of solidity."

According to the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, countries which want to join in the common currency must meet strict economic goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public borrowing in 1997.

With most core countries pretty much on target for the first three criteria, budgetary guidelines have been thrust into the spotlight, particularly as some countries turned to one-off income or deferred payments to make the grade in 1997.
But Spain appears to be faring well by comparison.
Although markets took a breather on Thursday after a leap higher on Wednesday, dealers saw further gains ahead.
"We can probably correct some and then turn around and rise later in the afternoon," a dealer said on Thursday.
